Name: safety_canary_gated_finetuning
Title: Watching Safety Erode in Real Time: Canary-Gated Fine-Tuning that Detects and Halts Alignment Collapse as It Happens
Short Hypothesis: Benign fine-tuning erodes safety not instantaneously but as a progressive trajectory. We hypothesize that a tiny set of held-out 'canary' probes, whose internal harmfulness-recognition signal is monitored at every optimizer step, provides an early-warning of impending alignment collapse many steps before behavioral safety actually breaks, and that a lightweight, drift-velocity-gated activation-anchoring intervention applied only when erosion is detected can preserve safety with far lower alignment tax than static parameter-freezing defenses that fail due to alternative pathways and second-order curvature dynamics.
Related Work: Static defenses freeze safety-critical parameters (SPPFT, SSAH), constrain updates along an alignment direction (AsFT), regularize safety-token confidence (Few Tokens Big Leverage), or prune harmful weights post-hoc (Antidote, SPLoRA). However, (a) the multilingual SIL work shows freezing safety parameters fails due to 'alternative pathways'; (b) 'The Geometry of Alignment Collapse' proves orthogonality-based static defenses collapse under second-order gradient-descent curvature, with a quartic scaling law in training time; (c) 'From Parameter Dynamics to Risk Scoring' shows safety erodes as cumulative drift toward danger-aligned directions, and scores samples but does not intervene during training. All prior defenses act on a static snapshot (initial parameters, a fixed direction, or post-hoc). Our proposal is distinct: it is a *training-time dynamical monitor + gated intervention* that (1) tracks the model's internal harmfulness-recognition signal on held-out canary probes at every step to forecast collapse before it manifests behaviorally, and (2) triggers a targeted activation-space anchoring/KL correction only when the erosion velocity exceeds threshold. By operating on behavior/activations rather than a fixed parameter set, it sidesteps the alternative-pathways failure mode; by acting dynamically it counters the second-order curvature drift that static methods cannot detect; and by gating it minimizes alignment tax versus always-on constraints. Concretely our delta is twofold and we keep the two contributions separate: (i) a detector contribution -- held-out canary probes read at every optimizer step give an internal-state early-warning signal unavailable to standard end-of-epoch safety evals, framed as a formal lead-time prediction problem; and (ii) an intervention contribution -- a drift-velocity-gated correction. Relative to Learning to Stay Safe and LARF (representation-level restoration) and parameter-dynamics risk scoring (which scores samples but never intervenes during training), the novelty is the online, gated coupling of detection to a conditional correction inside the fine-tuning loop.
Abstract: Fine-tuning an aligned LLM on even entirely benign data reliably erodes its safety guardrails. Recent mechanistic work reveals this is not an instantaneous event but a dynamical process: gradient descent steers parameters and activations progressively toward danger-aligned directions, driven by second-order curvature that static orthogonality- or freezing-based defenses provably cannot detect. We propose to defend where the damage actually unfolds: inside the fine-tuning loop, in real time. Our method, Canary-Gated Fine-Tuning (CGFT), inserts a small held-out set of 'safety canary' probes and, at every optimizer step, reads the model's internal harmfulness-recognition signal on them (projection onto a harmfulness direction plus refusal-token confidence) without contributing these probes to the task gradient. We show this canary signal drops with substantial lead time before behavioral safety (measured on separate attack sets) breaks, yielding an early-warning trajectory. When the erosion velocity exceeds a threshold, CGFT triggers a lightweight, gated intervention: a KL-anchor to the aligned reference model restricted to safety-relevant tokens plus a small activation nudge re-aligning the canary representations to their pre-fine-tuning geometry. Because the trigger is behavioral and dynamic, it evades the alternative-pathways and curvature failure modes of static defenses, and because it is gated it engages only when needed, minimizing alignment tax. We evaluate on Llama-3-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Gemma-2-9B across benign (Alpaca, Dolly, domain SFT), outlier-benign, and lightly poisoned fine-tuning, measuring canary early-warning lead time, post-fine-tuning attack success rate, downstream task performance, and over-refusal, comparing against SPPFT, AsFT, safety-token regularization, and Antidote. In a fine-tuning-as-a-service pipeline the canary runs as a cheap per-step forward pass on ~100 fixed probes, letting an operator halt or correct a run before it ships an unsafe model; we report this per-step overhead and frame the contribution as predictive monitoring plus conditional control rather than a new mechanistic theory.
Experiments:
Models throughout: Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Gemma-2-9B-IT. Fine-tuning is run both as LoRA (rank 16, alpha 32) and as full fine-tuning, at learning rates {1e-5, 5e-5, 2e-4}, up to 3 epochs, batch size 16, 3 seeds; the aligned pre-fine-tuning checkpoint is kept frozen as a reference. "Behavioral collapse" is defined before any run as the first optimizer step at which attack success rate (ASR) on a held-out attack eval rises >=20 points above the pre-fine-tuning ASR. The canary signal is the projection of canary activations onto a harmfulness direction (difference-in-means at the last instruction token) plus refusal-token confidence at the first response token; canary probes never contribute to the task gradient.

Experiment 1 (H1 — the canary signal gives early warning of alignment collapse many steps before behavioral safety breaks). Tests whether the canary signal drops with substantial lead time before behavioral collapse, and whether a detector on canary drift features predicts collapse ahead of time. Data: a held-out canary set of ~50 harmful and ~50 benign probe prompts (100 total), disjoint from all training and eval data, spanning HarmBench/StrongREJECT categories; fine-tuning corpora = Alpaca (we sample 5,000 instructions), Dolly (5,000), a domain SFT set (5,000 from a medical or code SFT corpus), an outlier-benign set (Self-Inf-N style, 2,000), and lightly poisoned variants injecting 1%, 3%, and 5% harmful examples into Alpaca; behavioral eval = ASR on 100 held-out HarmBench behaviors under direct request plus GCG and AutoDAN. Every 20 optimizer steps we log the canary signal (no gradient) and the behavioral ASR. Predictor: a threshold/logistic detector on canary drift features (value, velocity, curvature over a sliding window) trained to predict collapse M steps ahead, 3 seeds; trained on some datasets/models and tested on held-out ones. Baselines: a parameter-drift risk score (SQSD-style) and, as an oracle-cost reference, a per-step full safety eval. Decisive metric first: mean lead-time (optimizer steps between the canary alarm firing at 1% FPR and behavioral collapse), then predictor AUROC and TPR@1%FPR, then cross-dataset/cross-model consistency of the lead-time. Convincing result: the canary alarm precedes behavioral collapse by >=50 optimizer steps on average with predictor AUROC >=0.85, holding on the poisoned and outlier-benign runs as well as the clean ones. Indecision band (before data): mean lead-time in [10, 50] steps means the warning is real but short — H1 holds weakly and the gated intervention below must react within a few steps to be useful; lead-time is reported per dataset because it may vary. Negative result: lead-time <=0 (the canary signal drops at or after behavioral collapse) on most datasets means the canary lags rather than leads and H1 is unsupported.

Experiment 2 (H2 — canary-gated anchoring preserves safety at lower alignment tax than static defenses). Tests whether triggering a KL-anchor plus activation nudge only when canary drift velocity exceeds threshold keeps post-fine-tuning safety while costing less downstream performance than parameter-freezing/constraint defenses. Method: when canary drift velocity exceeds the threshold, add for that step (i) a KL-anchor loss to the frozen aligned reference restricted to safety-relevant response tokens and (ii) an activation nudge pulling canary representations toward their pre-fine-tuning geometry; the intervention gates off below threshold. Data: the fine-tuning corpora and behavioral eval from Experiment 1; downstream task accuracy on the dataset-specific metric or MMLU (2,000-subset)/GSM8K (1,319 test)/HumanEval (164); over-refusal on XSTest-safe (200) and OR-Bench-Hard-1K (500 sampled); general utility on MT-Bench (80) and AlpacaEval (805). Systems compared: no defense, CGFT (ours), SPPFT (freeze safety layers), AsFT (alignment-direction constraint), safety-token confidence regularization, and Antidote (post-hoc pruning). We sweep the gating threshold to trace the safety-vs-task Pareto and ablate KL-anchor vs. activation-nudge vs. both. Decisive metric first: post-fine-tuning ASR at matched downstream task accuracy; then over-refusal and general utility. Convincing result: CGFT holds post-fine-tuning ASR within 5 points of the pre-fine-tuning aligned model while downstream task accuracy stays within 2 points of undefended fine-tuning, dominating SPPFT/AsFT/safety-token-reg/Antidote on the ASR-vs-task frontier, with over-refusal rise <=5 points. Indecision band (before data): post-fine-tuning ASR within [5, 15] points of the aligned baseline, or a task-accuracy drop in [2, 5] points, means CGFT trades safety for utility rather than dominating — reported as a Pareto point. Negative result: ASR >15 points above the aligned baseline (safety not preserved) or a task drop >5 points (tax too high) means CGFT fails its purpose, falsifying H2.

Experiment 3 (H2 — robustness to aggressive fine-tuning and to a canary-aware attacker). Tests whether CGFT survives the high-learning-rate/high-epoch regime that breaks static defenses, and an attacker who suppresses canary drift while poisoning. Data: the 3%/5% poisoned Alpaca sets re-run at the highest learning rate (2e-4) and up to 5 epochs; plus an adaptive-poison variant that regularizes toward small canary drift. Systems compared: CGFT vs. SPPFT/AsFT/Antidote under the aggressive schedule. Decisive metric first: post-fine-tuning ASR under the aggressive schedule; then, for the adaptive attacker, the poison fraction required to reach a fixed ASR under CGFT vs. no defense. Convincing result: CGFT keeps post-fine-tuning ASR within 10 points of the aligned baseline where static defenses exceed +25 points, and the canary-aware attacker needs >=2x the poison fraction to reach the same ASR (raised attack cost is the intended outcome). Indecision band (before data): if CGFT's ASR lands within [10, 20] points of the aligned baseline under the aggressive schedule, it is partially robust — reported honestly, with the learning-rate regime where step-wise detection can no longer react noted as a limit. Negative result: CGFT's ASR indistinguishable from the static defenses under the aggressive schedule means real-time gating provides no advantage in that regime.

Experiment 4 (controls isolating the value of gating and probe design). Tests whether the gating (not just the correction components) and the internal canary (not just any held-out trigger) carry the benefit. Data/setup as in Experiment 2 on the three models. Gating-isolation arms, all using the same KL-anchor+nudge components: (a) always-on KL-anchor, (b) always-on nudge, (c) periodic (fixed-schedule) intervention, (d) random-trigger intervention matched in firing rate to CGFT, and (e) an external-eval-trigger that fires on a held-out behavioral safety eval instead of the internal canary. Probe-design ablations: canary-set size (10/25/50/100), category coverage, a random-probe set, and held-out harm categories absent from the canary. Decisive metric first: post-fine-tuning ASR at matched downstream task accuracy for each arm vs. gated CGFT; then the canary lead-time as a function of probe-set size/composition. Convincing result: gated CGFT matches or beats the always-on arms on the ASR-vs-task frontier while intervening on <=30% of steps, beats the random-trigger arm by >=10 ASR points at matched task accuracy, and the internal canary gives >=20 steps more lead-time than the external-eval trigger at equal compute; lead-time degrades gracefully down to a 25-probe set. Indecision band (before data): gated CGFT within [0, 10] ASR points of the best always-on arm means gating saves compute but not safety -- reported as such. Negative result: gated CGFT no better than the random-trigger arm means the canary signal, not the correction, was doing nothing, undercutting the detector claim.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) A small fixed canary set may not cover the space of safety behaviors, so erosion in uncovered categories could go undetected; mitigated by category-diverse canaries but not fully solved. 2) The canary signal might lag rather than lead behavioral collapse for some datasets, weakening early-warning value; the trajectory study directly tests this. 3) A single harmfulness direction may be insufficient (multi-dimensional safety), requiring subspace projections. 4) The gated intervention could increase over-refusal or reduce downstream performance if triggered too aggressively; the Pareto sweep quantifies this. 5) At very high learning rates collapse may be too fast for step-wise detection to react in time; robustness tests probe this regime. 6) Directions, thresholds, and gains are model-specific and need per-model calibration. 7) Determined adaptive attackers could suppress canary drift, though this appears to raise attack cost.
